html:
The shipping of about 60,000 Indian labourers to Fiji between 1879 and 1916 to work on sugar plantations. Their descendants, the Indo-Fijians, became a large part of the nation.

The first ship, the Leonidas, landed in May 1879. Governor Arthur Gordon wanted plantation labour without putting Fijians to work, and the measles epidemic had cut the local population. He copied the system of Indian indenture already used in Mauritius and the Caribbean.

Workers signed a five year contract, the girmit (from "agreement"), so they called themselves girmitiyas. Most worked cane for the Colonial Sugar Refining Company. Pay was low, punishments harsh and women few. Campaigners in India, inspired by Gandhi's fight in South Africa, pressed to end the system. Shipments stopped in 1916 and all contracts were cancelled in 1920.

Most girmitiyas stayed, leasing land and farming cane. By the middle of the 1900s Indo-Fijians outnumbered native Fijians. Tension over land and power led to the coups of 1987 and later, and many Indo-Fijians have since emigrated.
